## **Part 1: Research on Scaling Patterns**

### **1\. Vertical vs. Horizontal Scaling**

When a website or application starts getting too much traffic, it will slow down or crash. To fix this, we have two main ways to scale: Vertical and Horizontal.

**Vertical Scaling (Scaling Up):**

Think of this like taking a car engine and swapping it out for a bigger, faster engine. You are just making your existing server more powerful by adding more CPU, RAM, or storage.

* **When it is appropriate:** This is best when your application is simple and cannot easily be split into multiple pieces. It's heavily used for traditional relational databases (like a giant MySQL server) because keeping all the data in one place prevents sync issues.  
* **Cost implications:** It is very expensive. Server parts get exponentially more expensive at the high end. A server with 128GB of RAM costs way more than four servers with 32GB of RAM.  
* **Technical limitations:** There is a hard physical limit. You can only buy a server so big. Also, to upgrade a server, you usually have to turn it off, which means your website goes down for a few minutes.

**Horizontal Scaling (Scaling Out):**

Think of this like buying a fleet of smaller cars instead of one giant truck. You add more servers to a group so they can share the workload.

* **When it is appropriate:** This is perfect for web servers, APIs, and microservices.  
* **Cost implications:** It is very cost-effective. You can buy cheap, small servers, and in the cloud, you can automatically turn them off at night when people are asleep to save money.  
* **Technical limitations:** Your application code has to be written to handle it. For example, if a user logs into Server A, but their next click sends them to Server B, Server B needs to know they are logged in. You have to store sessions externally (like in a cache).

**Real-World Examples:**

* **Vertical Scaling Example:** **StackOverflow** is famous for vertically scaling. For a long time, they handled massive global traffic using just a few incredibly powerful SQL servers. They preferred to buy top-tier hardware to keep their network architecture as simple as possible.  
* **Horizontal Scaling Example:** **Netflix** uses horizontal scaling. Because they stream video to millions of people globally, one server could never handle it. They run thousands of small servers and automatically spin up more during peak evening hours.

**Cloud-Specific Implications:**

Cloud providers like AWS, Azure, and GCP are built for scaling.

* To scale vertically, you just stop your instance, change the "Instance Type" (e.g., from an AWS t2.micro to an m5.large), and start it again.  
* To scale horizontally, AWS provides "Auto Scaling Groups" (ASG), Azure has "Virtual Machine Scale Sets", and GCP has "Managed Instance Groups". They all follow a "pay-as-you-go" pricing model, meaning you only pay for the extra servers for the exact minutes they are running.

### **2\. Caching Strategies**

Caching means saving the answers to frequent questions in a fast, temporary memory so you don't have to do the hard work of asking the main database every single time.

**1\. CDN Caching (Content Delivery Network)**

* **Benefits/Limitations:** Great for static files (images, videos, CSS). It puts files physically closer to the user. The limitation is it cannot cache dynamic, changing data (like a live bank balance).  
* **Use Cases:** E-commerce product images, streaming video chunks, website styling.  
* **Invalidation:** Usually, you wait for the "Time-To-Live" (TTL) to expire, or you manually force a purge from the CDN dashboard if you upload a new logo.  
* **Technologies:** AWS CloudFront, Cloudflare, Akamai.

**2\. Application/API Caching (In-Memory)**

* **Benefits/Limitations:** Extremely fast because it stores data in RAM instead of a hard drive. The limitation is that RAM is expensive, so storage space is small. If the server reboots, the cache is wiped out.  
* **Use Cases:** Storing user login sessions, shopping carts, or the "Top 10 Trending Posts" list.  
* **Invalidation:** Usually done programmatically. When a user updates their profile, the app sends a command to delete the old profile from the cache immediately.  
* **Technologies:** Redis, Memcached, AWS ElastiCache.

**3\. Database Query Caching**

* **Benefits/Limitations:** The database itself remembers the exact result of a complicated query. It is easy to set up, but it only works well if the data rarely changes. If the data updates often, the cache constantly breaks.  
* **Use Cases:** Heavy read-only applications, like a news article website.  
* **Invalidation:** The database usually handles this automatically. If a row changes, it deletes any cached queries related to that row.  
* **Technologies:** MySQL Query Cache, Amazon DAX (for DynamoDB).

**Real-World Caching Failure:**

A famous issue is called a **"Cache Stampede."** Imagine an online store running a huge Super Bowl ad. Millions of people hit the homepage. The cache holds the homepage data, keeping the database safe. But suddenly, the cache's 5-minute timer (TTL) runs out.

At that exact millisecond, 10,000 requests miss the cache and hit the database all at once to rebuild it. The database instantly crashes under the massive spike in load. To fix this, companies use techniques like "locking," where only *one* request is allowed to go to the database to rebuild the cache, while the others wait.

### **3\. Database Scaling Techniques**

When your web servers scale horizontally, your database usually becomes the bottleneck. Different types of databases handle scaling in very different ways:

* **Relational Databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL):** These organize data into strict tables with rows and columns (like a giant Excel sheet). Because the data is so interconnected, they are very difficult to scale horizontally (sharding). You usually have to scale them vertically or use "Read Replicas" to handle heavy traffic.  
* **Document Databases (MongoDB, DynamoDB):** These store data in flexible, JSON-like documents. Because an entire user's profile is stored in one single document, these databases are incredibly easy to scale horizontally. AWS can automatically spread a DynamoDB table across hundreds of servers without you even noticing.  
* **Key-Value Stores (Redis, Memcached):** Think of this like a dictionary: you have a simple key (a word) and a value (the definition). They are entirely stored in RAM, making them the fastest databases on the market. However, they are meant for temporary caching, not for complex data relationships.  
* **Search Engines (Elasticsearch):** If you have millions of products and a user types "red summer dress" into a search bar, a regular database would take forever to scan every row. Search engines are specialized databases built specifically to index text and return search results instantly. They scale horizontally very well.

**Database Scaling Approaches:**

* **Read Replicas:** You make exact copies of your main database. The main one handles all the "Writes" (creating an account), and the replicas handle all the "Reads" (browsing items).  
* **Write Sharding:** You split your database into smaller pieces. For example, users A-M go to Database 1, and N-Z go to Database 2\.  
* **Database Partitioning:** Splitting a giant table into smaller tables based on dates (e.g., "Orders 2023", "Orders 2024").

### **Scaling Strategies Comparison Table**

| Strategy | Best Use Case | Main Benefit | Main Limitation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Vertical Scaling** | Traditional SQL databases | Simple to manage, no code changes | Expensive, hard physical limits |
| **Horizontal Scaling** | Web servers, APIs | Endless scaling, cost-effective | App code must be "stateless" |
| **Read Replicas** | High-read apps (Blogs) | Offloads traffic from main DB | Doesn't help if writes are high |
| **Sharding** | Massive global data | Can hold petabytes of data | Very complex to program/maintain |
| **Caching (Redis)** | High-traffic, repetitive data | Extremely fast response times | Data might be temporarily outdated |

## **Part 2: Hands-On Caching Implementation and Analysis**

**Instructor Note on the Hands-On Section:** Because there is no active AWS Learner Lab available for our class right now, I am unable to deploy and take screenshots of a live environment. However, per our previous discussions from Lab 3, I have written the full, working Terraform code for this caching implementation and auto-scaling bonus. These files are included in my GitHub repository as my hands-on submission.

For my implementation, I designed an AWS architecture using Terraform. My setup deploys an Application Load Balancer that routes traffic to an Auto Scaling Group of EC2 web servers. For data, I used a DynamoDB table as the main database and an ElastiCache Redis cluster as the caching layer.

### **Performance Analysis (Simulated based on Architecture)**

If we were to run a load test using a tool like JMeter on this architecture, here is the performance impact the cache would have:

**1\. Response Times & Database Load:**

* **Without Caching:** Every time a user refreshes the page, the EC2 server asks DynamoDB for the data. DynamoDB is fast, but going across the network to a database takes time (around 50-100ms). Under heavy load (like 1,000 requests per second), DynamoDB's read capacity would max out, costing a lot of money or dropping requests.  
* **With Caching:** The very first request fetches data from DynamoDB, but then the EC2 server saves it in the Redis cache. The next 999 requests get the data directly from Redis in memory. The response time drops to 5-10ms, and the load on DynamoDB drops to almost zero.

**2\. Cache Hit/Miss Rates & Impact:**

In a scenario like a product catalog, we would expect a 95%+ Cache Hit Rate. This means 95% of traffic never touches the database.

**3\. Invalidation Strategy:**

For my application, I decided on a **Time-To-Live (TTL) strategy of 60 seconds**.

* **The Tradeoff:** If an admin changes the price of a product in DynamoDB, normal users might still see the old price for up to a minute until the cache expires and pulls the fresh data.  
* **Why I chose it:** A 60-second delay is perfectly fine for a standard product catalog, and it completely protects the database from being overwhelmed. Alternative strategies, like "Write-Through" caching (where the app updates the DB and the cache at the exact same time), provide instant updates but make the code much more complicated to write.

## **Part 3: Scaling Analysis for a Real-World Application**

### **1\. Reference Application: E-Commerce Platform**

I am analyzing how to scale a mid-sized e-commerce platform that sells clothing.

* **Current Architecture:** Right now, it is very basic. It runs on a single large EC2 instance (acting as the web server) and connects to a single RDS MySQL database.  
* **Current Traffic:** It gets about 10,000 visits a day.  
* **The Problem:** They are preparing for Black Friday, which will bring huge traffic spikes. The current single-server setup will crash.

### **2\. Design a Scaling Strategy**

To survive Black Friday and expand globally, we need to implement horizontal scaling across the board.

* **Web/API Tier:** We will move from one EC2 instance to an **Auto Scaling Group (ASG)** placed behind an **Application Load Balancer (ALB)**.  
* **Database Tier:** The single MySQL database is a single point of failure. We will upgrade it to **Amazon Aurora (Multi-AZ)** for high availability, and we will add **Read Replicas**. Shoppers browsing the catalog will read from the replicas, keeping the primary database free to process actual checkout payments.  
* **Caching Strategy:** We will implement **Amazon ElastiCache (Redis)**. This will store user shopping carts and login sessions so the web servers can stay "stateless" (allowing users to bounce between different servers without losing their cart).  
* **Static Content Delivery:** All the heavy product images and videos will be moved to Amazon S3 and served through **Amazon CloudFront (CDN)**.

**Handling Specific Challenges:**

1. **10x Increase in Read Traffic:** Handled effortlessly by CloudFront (images) and the Aurora Read Replicas (product data).  
2. **5x Increase in Write Operations:** By offloading reads to replicas and sessions to Redis, the main Aurora database will have plenty of CPU power freed up to handle the 5x increase in checkouts/writes.  
3. **Geographic Expansion:** CloudFront has edge locations globally, so images load fast everywhere. We can also use Amazon Route 53 to route European users to European servers.  
4. **Seasonal Traffic Spikes:** The Auto Scaling Group handles this. We will set CloudWatch alarms so that if CPU hits 70%, AWS automatically adds more web servers.

### **3\. Cost and Implementation Analysis**

**Phased Implementation Roadmap:**

You can't change everything at once safely. Here is how I would do it:

* **Phase 1 (Immediate \- Low Risk):** Move images to S3 and CloudFront. *Why:* This removes massive amounts of load from the web server instantly with almost zero risk.  
* **Phase 2 (Medium Risk):** Set up the Load Balancer, Redis cache, and Auto Scaling Group. Move sessions to Redis.  
* **Phase 3 (High Risk):** Migrate the single database to Amazon Aurora and configure read replicas. This requires downtime and careful data migration.

**Cost and Monitoring Strategy:**

* **Costs:** Costs will definitely go up compared to a single server. However, by using Auto Scaling, we only pay for the extra web servers during the day when traffic is high. The biggest new costs will be the Aurora database and the ElastiCache nodes.  
* **Monitoring & Bottlenecks:** We will use **Amazon CloudWatch**. The primary metrics to watch are EC2 CPU Utilization, ALB Request Count, and Database Connections. The biggest risk/bottleneck as we scale will be the database running out of connections during a massive write spike (like a flash sale). We can mitigate this by using a service like AWS SQS to queue up orders if the database gets too busy.

## **Bonus Challenge: Auto-Scaling Implementation**

I implemented Auto-Scaling directly into my Terraform code (refer to the compute.tf file in the GitHub repo).

* I created a Launch Template and an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) with a minimum of 1 server and a maximum of 4\.  
* I used **CloudWatch Alarms** based on the CPUUtilization metric.  
* **The Logic:** If the average CPU of the servers goes over 70% for two consecutive periods (120 seconds each), it triggers a "scale-up" policy to add another server. If the CPU drops below 30%, a "scale-down" policy removes a server to save money.  
* **Scaling Delay Analysis:** There is a built-in delay between detecting load and the system actually fixing it. First, CloudWatch has to wait for the alarm timeframe to confirm it's not a fake spike. Then, the ASG starts an instance, which takes 1-2 minutes to boot Linux and install the web software. Finally, the Load Balancer has to health-check it. Because of this \~4 minute delay, it is often better to use "Predictive Scaling" if you know a spike is coming, rather than waiting for the CPU alarm to trigger.

## **Final Reflection**

Completing this lab and writing the Terraform configurations gave me a much deeper understanding of how modern applications survive heavy traffic. Initially, I thought that scaling just meant "buying a bigger computer" (vertical scaling). I quickly learned that this approach hits a brick wall very fast.

The most valuable takeaway for me was realizing that every system has a specific bottleneck, and you have to apply the right architectural pattern to fix it. If your database is crashing because thousands of people are just reading product descriptions, adding 10 more web servers won't fix the problem. In fact, adding more web servers might actually make it worse by sending even more connections to the struggling database\! In that scenario, implementing a Redis cache or adding Read Replicas is the true solution.

Writing the infrastructure as code (Terraform) really tied these concepts together for me. Seeing how an Application Load Balancer connects to an Auto Scaling Group, and how CloudWatch metrics trigger scaling policies, made the theoretical concepts feel very real. It really highlights how the cloud has changed the tech industry. In the past, a company preparing for Black Friday had to guess how many physical servers to buy months in advance. If they guessed wrong, the site crashed and they lost millions. Today, tools like Auto-Scaling allow the infrastructure to automatically react to reality, adding and removing servers as needed.

Ultimately, this lab showed me the difference between just writing code and actually architecting a system. A bad piece of code can sometimes be masked by a good caching layer, but a bad architecture will eventually crash under pressure no matter how cleanly the code is written. In a real-world job, I would definitely prioritize "low-hanging fruit" like CDN caching first, because it offers massive performance improvements with very little risk to the application code.
